newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: British woman wins fight for slice of inheritance.
newsitem.headline: British woman wins fight for slice of inheritance.

text.p: A British woman has won a two-year court battle in Singapore for a slice of her ex-husband's inheritance, her lawyer said on Thursday.
Singapore's court of appeal on Wednesday ruled in Jane Ong's favour for half of her ex-husband's portion of his family's estate, estimated to be worth at least US$50 million, lawyer Andre Arul said.

The actual value could be higher because the ex-husband's father, an Indonesian tycoon who died without a will in 1974, owned numerous properties and assets in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Hong Kong, Arul told Reuters.

The father, Ong Seng Keng, was founder of Indonesia's P.T. Bank Rama, and at the time of his death still owned 50 percent of the company. Since he died intestate, his estate is equally divided among his wife and three sons, Arul said.
Jane Ong, 36, would be given half of her ex-husband's share of his father's estate, which could be at least $12.5 million.
Jane Ong, whose maiden name is Butler, lives in London with her two sons and a daughter aged between 12 and 15 years.
She won the first legal battle in June last year when a high court ruled in her favour after a 33-day trial in which she argued her own case.
Her ex-husband, Ong Siauw Tjoan, 39, from whom she filed for divorce in 1988, and his mother Lim Lie Hoa, appealed against the decision. They live in Singapore.
A three-judge court, led by Chief Justice Yong Pung How, on Wednesday dismissed the appeal after a two-day trial.

Jane Ong and Ong Siauw Tjoan were married in London in 1982. In 1988 she obtained a maintenance order against Ong, who had repeatedly defaulted on payments to her and their children, Arul said. The debt amounted about 250,000 pounds sterling, Arul said.
Arul said Jane Ong has so far not received anything from her ex-husband, and would not until a judicial enquiry ascertains the actual value of the family estate.
The court has given Ong Siauw Tjoan and his mother until May 3 to clarify the family's accounts, the lawyer said.
